title: Transcendence is Preserved by Algebraic Operations: The Algebraic Numbers form a Subfield
description: Develops the arithmetic/field side of the algebraic–transcendental dichotomy, complementing the parent's countability result. For any field extension K ⊆ L, the elements algebraic over K form a subfield (algebraicSubfield K L), so the field of algebraic numbers is a countable subfield of ℂ. Dually, transcendence is preserved by every algebraic operation: if t is transcendental over K and a, b are algebraic over K, then t+a, a+t, t−a, a−t, t⁻¹, −t, tⁿ (n>0), a·t and t·a (a≠0), and the affine image a·t+b (a≠0) are all transcendental. A final contrast shows the transcendentals are NOT closed: t and 1−t are both transcendental but sum to the algebraic number 1.

overview.historicalContext: Cantor's 1874 result that the algebraic numbers are countable is a statement about cardinality. But the algebraic numbers carry far more structure: closed under the four field operations, they form the algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}$ inside $\mathbb{C}$ — a countable algebraically-closed field. The elementary first half of that structure (closure under $+,-,\times,{}^{-1}$) is also the standard opening move of every concrete transcendence proof: once a single number such as $e$ (Hermite 1873) is known transcendental, an entire algebraic orbit $e+1,\,e^2,\,1/e,\,2e-3,\ldots$ is transcendental for free. The structural facts isolated here are the elementary toolkit assumed at the start of Lindemann–Weierstrass, Gelfond–Schneider, and Baker's theorem; this entry makes that toolkit explicit and machine-checked.
overview.problemStatement: Develop the field-theoretic side of the algebraic–transcendental dichotomy, complementing the parent's countability theorem. (1) Show that for any field extension $K \subseteq L$ the elements of $L$ algebraic over $K$ form a subfield $\mathrm{algebraicSubfield}\,K\,L : \mathrm{Subfield}\,L$ (so the algebraic numbers are a countable subfield of $\mathbb{C}$). (2) Show that transcendence is preserved by every algebraic operation: if $t$ is transcendental over $K$ and $a,b$ are algebraic over $K$ then $t+a$, $a+t$, $t-a$, $a-t$, $t^{-1}$, $-t$, $t^n\,(n>0)$, $a\cdot t$ and $t\cdot a\,(a\ne 0)$, and the affine image $a\cdot t+b\,(a\ne 0)$ are all transcendental. (3) Contrast: the transcendentals are closed under none of these.
overview.proofStrategy:
**§1 — Subfield closure.** Over a field $K$, algebraicity coincides with integrality (`isAlgebraic_iff_isIntegral`). Each of $+,-,\times,\mathrm{neg}$ is proved by rewriting `IsAlgebraic` to `IsIntegral` on every hypothesis and the goal and invoking Mathlib's integral-closure subring lemmas (`IsIntegral.add/sub/mul/neg`); the inverse uses `IsAlgebraic.inv`. These six facts are bundled into `algebraicSubfield K L : Subfield L`, whose carrier is $\{x \mid \mathrm{IsAlgebraic}\,K\,x\}$.

**§2 — Transcendence preservation.** Every preservation theorem is a one-line *back-substitution* contradiction against §1. If $t+a$ were algebraic, then $t = (t+a)-a$ would be a difference of algebraics, hence algebraic by `isAlgebraic_sub` — contradicting `Transcendental K t`. Products use $t = a^{-1}\cdot(a\cdot t)$ with `inv_mul_cancel_left₀`; the subtraction/negation cases are `simpa [sub_eq_add_neg]` reductions to the additive case; powers reuse Mathlib's `Transcendental.pow`. The capstone `transcendental_affine` composes the multiplicative and additive translates.

**§3 — Non-closure.** For any transcendental $t$, `transcendental_algebraic_sub` makes $1-t$ transcendental, yet $t+(1-t)=1$ is algebraic (`ring` + `isAlgebraic_one`), so the transcendentals fail closure under addition.
keyInsights: **Transcendence preservation is the contrapositive of subfield closure.** If $t$ is transcendental and $a$ is algebraic, then $t+a$ cannot be algebraic, because otherwise $t=(t+a)-a$ would be a difference of two algebraic numbers, hence algebraic. The same back-substitution — using $a^{-1}$ for products and inverses — handles every operation in one line.

**Algebraic = integral over a field.** The closure proofs never touch minimal polynomials directly: `isAlgebraic_iff_isIntegral` transports the whole problem into the integral-closure world, where Mathlib already knows the integral elements form a subring. The field hypothesis on $K$ is exactly what makes this bridge available.

**A subfield and its complement behave oppositely.** The algebraic numbers are closed under all field operations; the transcendentals, being the set-theoretic complement of a nontrivial subfield, are closed under none. $t$ and $1-t$ transcendental with algebraic sum $1$ is the cleanest witness.

**One affine theorem packages the whole toolkit.** `transcendental_affine` ($t \mapsto a\cdot t+b$, $a\ne 0$, $a,b$ algebraic) subsumes the additive and multiplicative translates and is the form actually invoked in transcendence arguments — it says the transcendentals are invariant under every algebraic affine map.

**Upgrading 'countable set' to 'countable subfield'.** Combined with the parent's countability result, `algebraicSubfield ℚ ℂ` is a countable subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ — the first structural step toward recognizing $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ as a countable algebraically closed field.

sections.title: §1: The algebraic numbers form a subfield
sections.summary: Closure of algebraicity under +, -, *, neg and ⁻¹, packaged as algebraicSubfield K L : Subfield L. The four ring operations are proved by rewriting IsAlgebraic to IsIntegral (valid since K is a field) and invoking Mathlib's integral-closure subring lemmas; the inverse uses IsAlgebraic.inv.
sections.mathContext: For a field extension K ⊆ L the integral and algebraic elements coincide. Mathlib already proves the integral elements form a subring (IsIntegral.add/sub/mul/neg), and that the inverse of an algebraic element of a field extension is algebraic, so all six subfield axioms are available.

sections.title: §2: Transcendence is preserved by algebraic operations
sections.summary: Eleven preservation theorems: additive translates (t+a, a+t, t−a, a−t), nonzero rescalings (a·t, t·a), inversion (t⁻¹), negation (−t), positive powers (tⁿ), and the capstone affine map a·t+b. Each is a one-line contradiction from §1's closure lemmas.
sections.mathContext: These are exactly the closure facts the algebraic toolkit supplies to transcendence theory: the set of transcendentals is invariant under every algebraic affine map x ↦ a·x + b with a ≠ 0 and a, b algebraic.

sections.title: §3: The transcendentals are NOT closed
sections.summary: transcendentals_not_add_closed: for any transcendental t, both t and 1−t are transcendental, yet t + (1−t) = 1 is algebraic. The transcendentals therefore form no subfield — they are the complement of the algebraic subfield of §1.
sections.mathContext: The asymmetry is structural: the algebraic numbers are a subfield, the transcendentals are its complement, and a complement of a nontrivial subfield is never closed under the field operations.

sections.title: §4: Sanity checks over ℚ ⊆ ℂ
sections.summary: Concrete instantiations at K = ℚ, L = ℂ for an arbitrary transcendental t: t+1, t⁻¹, t², and 1−t are transcendental — demonstrating the general theorems on the field of complex numbers.
sections.mathContext: Witnesses for such t are guaranteed by the sibling leaves (uncountably many transcendental reals/complexes); classical examples include e and any Liouville number.

conclusion.summary: Beyond being a countable set, the algebraic numbers form a subfield of ℂ (algebraicSubfield), and transcendence is preserved under every field operation — addition/subtraction by an algebraic, multiplication/division by a nonzero algebraic, inversion, negation, positive powers, and arbitrary algebraic affine maps a·t+b. Dually, the transcendentals are closed under none of these: t and 1−t are transcendental but sum to the algebraic number 1. The algebraic numbers are the subfield; the transcendentals are exactly its complement.
implications: Upgrades the parent's 'the algebraic numbers are a countable set' to 'a countable subfield of ℂ', the first structural step toward recognizing $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$ as a countable algebraically closed field.

Supplies the elementary closure toolkit every concrete transcendence proof opens with: once one number (e.g. $e$, $\pi$, a Liouville number) is known transcendental, its entire algebraic affine orbit is transcendental for free.
Explains structurally why the transcendentals are not a field — they are the complement of the algebraic subfield, and the complement of a nontrivial subfield is closed under no field operation.
openQuestions: Strengthen algebraicSubfield to an IntermediateField and prove it is algebraically closed (the algebraic closure of ℚ in ℂ).
Connect the affine-orbit structure to concrete transcendence statements such as Lindemann–Weierstrass ($e^{\alpha}$ transcendental for nonzero algebraic $\alpha$) and Gelfond–Schneider.
Quantify the field of algebraic numbers as a countable algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, identifying it up to isomorphism with $\overline{\mathbb{Q}}$.

mainTheorems.name: algebraicSubfield
mainTheorems.description: The elements of L algebraic over K, assembled as a subfield of L. Instantiated at K = ℚ, L = ℂ it is the field of algebraic numbers, which the parent proves countable.

mainTheorems.name: transcendental_affine
mainTheorems.description: For a ≠ 0 and a, b algebraic over K, the algebraic affine map t ↦ a·t + b sends every transcendental to a transcendental. Packages the additive and multiplicative preservation results.
mainTheorems.leanType: Transcendental K t → IsAlgebraic K a → IsAlgebraic K b → a ≠ 0 → Transcendental K (a * t + b)

mainTheorems.name: transcendental_add_algebraic
mainTheorems.description: A transcendental plus an algebraic is transcendental, by the back-substitution t = (t + a) − a.
mainTheorems.leanType: Transcendental K t → IsAlgebraic K a → Transcendental K (t + a)

mainTheorems.name: transcendental_algebraic_mul
mainTheorems.description: A nonzero algebraic times a transcendental is transcendental, by t = a⁻¹ · (a · t).
mainTheorems.leanType: Transcendental K t → IsAlgebraic K a → a ≠ 0 → Transcendental K (a * t)

mainTheorems.name: transcendental_inv
mainTheorems.description: The inverse of a transcendental element is transcendental.
mainTheorems.leanType: Transcendental K t → Transcendental K t⁻¹

mainTheorems.name: transcendentals_not_add_closed
mainTheorems.description: The transcendentals form no subfield: t and 1−t are transcendental, yet their sum 1 is algebraic.
mainTheorems.leanType: Transcendental K t → Transcendental K (1 - t) ∧ IsAlgebraic K (t + (1 - t))

mainTheorems.name: isAlgebraic_mul
mainTheorems.description: Product of algebraic elements is algebraic (one of the four subfield-closure lemmas), via integral closure.
mainTheorems.leanType: IsAlgebraic K x → IsAlgebraic K y → IsAlgebraic K (x * y)
